screens.title: Operators and Control Structures
screens.subtitle: Manipulate values and direct execution safely and efficiently in Solidity

narration.text: In this chapter you will learn how to change and check values, and how to make your contract decide what to do next. Operators are the building blocks for arithmetic, comparisons, logical decisions and bitwise manipulation. Control structures, like if/else and loops, let you run code conditionally or repeatedly. Both ideas are core to writing responsive contract logic, but on-chain they also carry gas costs and safety implications. For example, arithmetic in Solidity 0.8.0 and later reverts on overflow, preventing silent errors. Short-circuiting in logical expressions can save gas by avoiding expensive second checks. And loops that iterate over unbounded data can run out of gas and break your contract. You will see concrete code examples, a small access control exercise, and practical alternatives—like mappings and pagination—for common patterns. By the end of this lesson, you’ll understand the operators available, how to write clear conditionals, and how to choose loop patterns that avoid costly failures. Consider what part of your contract might unexpectedly loop over many items; that is where gas-aware design matters most.

keyIdea.text: Operators and control structures shape safety, correctness, and gas cost. Small choices here prevent reverts and vulnerabilities.

narration.text: This first set of objectives focuses on operator use and basic control flow. You will learn to apply arithmetic, comparison, logical, and bitwise operators in Solidity expressions and understand their direct effect on contract state and boolean outcomes. You will implement conditional logic using if, else if, and else, which allows your contract to choose different execution paths based on on-chain conditions like msg. sender or numeric thresholds. Each objective links a skill to a reason: for example, using comparison operators correctly prevents false access grants; using bitwise flags can pack state efficiently. You will also practice short-circuiting in logical expressions so that expensive evaluations are avoided when unnecessary, saving gas. A short mnemonic and a small visual cue on each objective will help you remember the skill pattern. By working through these concrete objectives, you’ll be prepared to reason about expressions and structure conditionals in a way auditors and users expect. Try naming one conditional in your contract and ask whether evaluating its second operand could be skipped to save gas.

narration.text: This second set of objectives extends your operator and control knowledge into practical patterns and gas-safety. You will utilize short-circuiting to avoid evaluating costly expressions when the first operand already determines the outcome. Practically, that means placing cheap checks first and expensive ones second in an AND or OR expression. You will also adopt data-structure choices that replace iteration with constant-time membership tests, for example using a mapping to check participation instead of scanning a large array. The chapter asks you to implement a simple admin-only action and to consider patterns like pagination and batch processing when work could be large. Finally, you will learn to reason about common mistakes—such as nested conditionals that are hard to audit or loops that unintentionally iterate over very large arrays—and how to refactor them. screens.title: Operator Categories in Solidity
screens.subtitle: What operators exist and what each category does

narration.text: Operators in Solidity fall into clear categories that map directly to common programming needs. Arithmetic operators—addition, subtraction, multiplication, division and modulo—compute numeric results. Comparison operators produce boolean outcomes and include equals, not-equals, less-than and greater-than families. Logical operators combine boolean expressions with AND, OR and NOT semantics and are crucial for writing compound checks. Bitwise operators operate on integer bits to implement flags or compact state. Each category matters for different reasons: arithmetic changes numeric state, comparisons gate flow, logical operators combine conditions, and bitwise operations let you pack several flags into a single integer to save storage cost. A common misconception is to treat bitwise tricks as universally better; while they save storage, they can reduce clarity. Another misconception is assuming logical operators always evaluate both sides; in Solidity, AND and OR short-circuit, which affects both correctness and gas cost. A concrete example is using a mapping to check membership instead of scanning an array—this is enabled by comparison and boolean logic rather than arithmetic. Takeaway: recognize which operator family maps to your intent—compute values, compare values, combine tests, or manipulate bits—and choose the clearest form for security and gas efficiency.

keyIdea.title: Operator families
keyIdea.text: Arithmetic, comparison, logical and bitwise operators each serve distinct roles—pick the right family for clarity, security, and gas-efficiency.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Operator Categories
Definition

Operator families

Simple descriptions link each operator category to the programmer intent and typical use-cases on-chain.

Quick reference
  • Arithmetic: +, -, *, /, %
  • Comparison: ==, !=, <, >, <=, >=
  • Logical: &&, ||, ! (short-circuiting applies)
  • Bitwise: &, |, ^, ~, <<, >>
Example

Use comparison and logical operators to check if msg.sender is authorized and a numeric threshold is met before proceeding.

Key Takeaway

Match operator type to intent: computation, test, combination, or bit manipulation. Clarity beats clever packing when security is at stake.

Annotated examples
Arithmetic snippet
uint sum = a + b;
uint product = a * b;
uint remainder = a % b;
Logical & Comparison
if (caller == owner && value > 100) {
  // proceed
}
Misconception

Bitwise tricks save storage but reduce readability. Short-circuiting means second operands may not run—don’t rely on side effects there.

screens.title: Arithmetic Operators and Overflow Safety (Solidity 0.8.0+)
screens.subtitle: How arithmetic works and why 0.8.0+ behavior matters

narration.text: Arithmetic operators perform the basic numeric computations your contract needs, and Solidity 0.8.0 and later adds automatic overflow and underflow checks that revert on invalid arithmetic. That change prevents silent wrapping bugs that used to be common. Practically, when you add or multiply two uint values that would exceed the maximum representable value, the transaction reverts and state is not changed. For example, multiplying a very large uint by two can exceed the allowed range and will cause a revert. A misconception is assuming overflow still wraps quietly; it does not in modern Solidity. Another important point for smart contracts is to avoid relying on gas-heavy arithmetic patterns inside large loops—each operation costs gas. The chapter provides a safe performCalculations function that uses addition, multiplication and modulo; when you test arithmetic in Remix, observe revert behavior by passing values that exceed the type limits. Concrete example: computing a product where a equals two to the power of 255 and b equals two results in an overflow that reverts, preserving contract correctness. Takeaway: write arithmetic with the expectation that invalid math triggers a revert and design guards or checks accordingly.

keyIdea.title: Overflow safety
keyIdea.text: Solidity 0.8.0+ reverts on overflow/underflow—this prevents silent errors but requires you to handle or avoid invalid arithmetic.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Arithmetic & Overflow
Code example
// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
pragma solidity ^0.8.0;

function performCalculations(uint a, uint b) pure returns (uint sum, uint product, uint remainder) {
  sum = a + b;
  product = a * b;
  remainder = a % b;
  // In 0.8.0+, overflow or underflow will revert the transaction.
}
Try feeding large values to observe revert behavior. Design guards or pre-checks for values that might overflow.
Concrete example

If a = 2**255 and b = 2, the multiplication a * b equals 2**256 and will exceed uint256 max, causing a revert in Solidity 0.8.0+.

Common mistake

Assuming arithmetic wraps silently. Modern Solidity reverts instead, so runtime checks and tests are essential.

Key Takeaway

Expect reverts on invalid arithmetic. Test edge values and avoid risky arithmetic inside unbounded loops.

screens.title: Comparison Operators and Boolean Results
screens.subtitle: Using comparisons to control contract decisions

narration.text: Comparison operators compare two values and return a boolean result that you can use to make decisions. Operators such as equals, not-equals, less-than and greater-than let your contract check conditions like ownership, balances or thresholds. For example, using a comparison to confirm that a caller equals an owner is a common access control pattern. Remember that comparisons return a true or false value and should be combined with logical operators when you need compound checks. A common misconception is mixing type sizes or signedness without considering the comparison semantics; always ensure both operands are comparable types. When composing comparisons with logical operators, bear in mind short-circuiting: the second part might not run if the first determines the result, which both saves gas and affects side-effect expectations. Concrete example: checking if an address is the admin can be expressed as address == admin; combine that with a value check to require both conditions. Takeaway: use explicit comparisons to make your contract's intent verifiable and pair them with clear logical structure so they remain auditable and gas-efficient. Comparison Operators and Boolean Results means comparisons return booleans used to gate behavior—use them explicitly and pair with clear logical structure to avoid mistakes.. In practical terms, using comparisons to control contract decisions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Comparison essentials
keyIdea.text: Comparisons return booleans used to gate behavior—use them explicitly and pair with clear logical structure to avoid mistakes.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Comparison Operators
Examples and use

Comparison operators evaluate relations and return true or false. Common uses include access checks, threshold gates, and validation of inputs.

  • Access: caller == owner
  • Range checks: value >= minimum && value <= maximum
  • Equality vs identity: compare types carefully
Concrete snippet
function isAdmin(address _addr) public view returns (bool) {
  return (_addr == admin);
}
Misconception

Comparing mismatched types or expecting implicit conversions can lead to unexpected results. Be explicit in types and ranges.

Key Takeaway

Use clear comparisons for gate conditions and verify operand types to avoid subtle bugs.

screens.title: Logical Operators and Short-Circuiting
screens.subtitle: Combining boolean expressions while saving gas

narration.text: Logical operators combine boolean expressions to form compound conditions. The AND operator requires both sides to be true, OR requires at least one true operand, and NOT flips a boolean. In Solidity, AND and OR short-circuit: when the first operand determines the result, the second operand is not evaluated. This behavior can be used intentionally to avoid expensive checks or calls. For instance, checking a cheap equality first can prevent an expensive storage read or call in the second operand. The contract example checkAccess shows this: when the first equality fails, the second comparison is never evaluated. A common misconception is relying on side effects in the second operand—because it might not run, you should not depend on side effects inside boolean operands. Another point is gas ordering: arrange conditions by cost, cheap-to-evaluate first. A concrete pattern: place ownership or index bounds checks before any heavy computation or storage access inside the same conditional. Takeaway: short-circuiting is both a gas optimization tool and a control-flow consideration—use it to reduce cost and avoid unintended reliance on skipped side effects. Logical Operators and Short-Circuiting means order conditional checks by cost and never place required side effects in operands that may be skipped.. In practical terms, combining boolean expressions while saving gas. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Short-circuiting matters
keyIdea.text: Order conditional checks by cost and never place required side effects in operands that may be skipped.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Logical Operators
Illustration
function checkAccess(address _caller, uint _value) view returns (bool) {
  if (_caller == owner && _value > 100) {
    return true;
  } else if (_caller != owner && _value < 50) {
    return false;
  }
  return false;
}
Here, owner equality is cheap and can prevent evaluating value checks in many cases.
Concrete tip

Order boolean operands by expected cost: cheapest first to maximize skipped evaluations and save gas.

Misconception

Never rely on side effects inside boolean operands because short-circuiting may skip them.

Key Takeaway

Short-circuiting is a tool. Use operand ordering for gas savings and avoid embedding required side effects in conditions.

screens.title: Bitwise Operators and Flags
screens.subtitle: Packing state and checking flags with bit operations

narration.text: Bitwise operators manipulate the individual bits of integer values and are commonly used for compact state or flag management. Operators like AND, OR, XOR, NOT and the left/right shifts let you set, clear and test specific bits. For example, using an 8-bit flags variable you can represent up to eight independent boolean flags, setting a bit with flags |= (1 << n) and checking with (flags & (1 << n))!= 0. The chapter's setFlag and isFlagSet functions demonstrate this pattern. Bitwise operations are efficient for storage cost, but they reduce human readability and can complicate audits. A misconception is that bitwise packing always improves safety; it improves cost but may increase the chance of logic errors if masks are wrong. Use bitwise flags where compactness matters and document which bit represents what. Concrete example: setFlag(3) sets the fourth bit so you can later check isFlagSet(3). Takeaway: bitwise operations are a low-level tool for optimization—use them intentionally and with clear documentation. Bitwise Operators and Flags means bitwise operators pack multiple booleans into one integer—powerful for optimization, but use with caution and documentation.. In practical terms, packing state and checking flags with bit operations. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Bitwise flags
keyIdea.text: Bitwise operators pack multiple booleans into one integer—powerful for optimization, but use with caution and documentation.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Bitwise Operators
Flag pattern
uint8 flags = 0; // 00000000

function setFlag(uint8 bit) public {
  require(bit < 8);
  flags |= (1 << bit);
}

function isFlagSet(uint8 bit) public view returns (bool) {
  require(bit < 8);
  return (flags & (1 << bit)) != 0;
}
When to use

Use bitwise flags when you need compact storage for many boolean attributes and can accept lower readability.

Common mistake

Misindexing bits or misapplying masks can silently break logic. Always document which bit maps to which flag.

Key Takeaway

Bitwise ops are efficient but low-level. Use them when storage economy matters and keep clear documentation to avoid errors.

screens.title: If / Else If / Else — Clear Conditional Design
screens.subtitle: Writing readable and auditable branching logic

narration.text: If, else if and else are the primary tools for conditional branching in Solidity. Use them to express mutually exclusive cases and to provide a safe default when none of the conditions match. The getStatusMessage example demonstrates mapping a status id to a human-readable string using a sequence of checks. Keep conditionals shallow and descriptive to reduce audit complexity. Deep nesting increases cognitive load and can hide edge cases. A common pitfall is writing many nested if blocks that handle similar cases; often a clearer structure or a mapping lookup is better. For example, instead of nested checks for multiple status codes, consider a mapping from id to string or an enumerated type to make the logic explicit. Another practical tip is to fail early: check and revert on invalid inputs first, then proceed to the main logic. This approach reduces possible state changes under invalid conditions and makes the happy path more visible. Takeaway: design conditionals for readability, auditability and safety—choose data-driven patterns when many cases exist. If / Else If / Else — Clear Conditional Design means prefer flat, data-driven conditionals and early-failure checks to nested branches for clarity and safety.. In practical terms, writing readable and auditable branching logic. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Readable branching
keyIdea.text: Prefer flat, data-driven conditionals and early-failure checks to nested branches for clarity and safety.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › If / Else
Example: status mapping via conditionals
function getStatusMessage(uint _statusId) public pure returns (string memory) {
  if (_statusId == 1) { return "Active"; }
  else if (_statusId == 2) { return "Paused"; }
  else { return "Unknown"; }
}
For many cases, a mapping or enum offers clearer intent and easier extension.
Practical tip

Fail early by validating inputs and revert on bad values before executing main logic to keep state consistent.

Misconception

Excessive nesting is a sign the design may be data-driven rather than conditional-driven. Consider mapping or enums for many discrete cases.

Key Takeaway

Write conditionals for clarity. Use enumerations or mappings instead of many nested ifs to keep code auditable and maintainable.

screens.title: For Loops and Gas Considerations
screens.subtitle: When loops are appropriate and patterns to avoid expensive iteration

narration.text: For loops iterate when you know the number of iterations or are iterating a fixed collection. In smart contracts, every loop iteration costs gas, so even a simple arithmetic inside a loop accumulates cost per step. The chapter demonstrates a calculateSum that iterates a small static array safely, but warns about iterating over dynamic arrays that can grow without bound. A common anti-pattern is scanning a dynamic or user-extendable array inside a single transaction; if the array grows large enough the transaction will run out of gas and revert. Safer alternatives include maintaining aggregates incrementally as items are added so you avoid full scans, exposing functions that process a fixed-size slice of data per call (pagination), or using mappings for constant-time membership checks instead of linear-time scans. Concrete example: if you need to check membership among thousands of addresses, use mapping(address => bool) to check in constant time rather than looping. Misconception: assuming that small loops remain safe as data grows; always design assuming data can grow and select patterns that scale. Takeaway: use for loops for bounded, predictable work and prefer batch or mapping patterns for large or evolving datasets.

keyIdea.title: Bounded iteration only
keyIdea.text: For loops are fine for known, small bounds. For dynamic or large data prefer aggregations, mappings, or batched processing to prevent out-of-gas failures.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › For Loops
Safe for loop example
uint[] public numbers = [1,2,3,4,5];
uint public sumOfNumbers = 0;

function calculateSum() public {
  sumOfNumbers = 0;
  for (uint i = 0; i < numbers.length; i++) {
    sumOfNumbers += numbers[i];
  }
}
This is safe for a small, known array. If numbers could be thousands long, this approach becomes unsafe.
Alternatives
  • Maintain running aggregates when items are added or removed
  • Process items in fixed-size batches across multiple transactions
  • Use mappings for membership checks instead of scanning arrays
Misconception

Assuming data size stays small. On-chain data can grow; design with scalability in mind from the start.

Key Takeaway

Avoid unbounded loops. If work could be large, pick aggregates, mappings, pagination, or batched processing instead.

screens.title: While Loops, Infinite Loops, and Safer Patterns
screens.subtitle: Understanding while loops and why boundedness matters on-chain

narration.text: While loops repeat until a condition becomes false. They are flexible but potentially dangerous on-chain because the number of iterations depends on runtime state. The countdown example in the chapter shows a safe bounded use where the loop reduces a local counter until it reaches zero. But imagine if the loop condition depends on an external, unbounded dataset or a user input that never changes: the loop could run too long, consume gas, and cause the transaction to fail. A common error is not guaranteeing progress toward the termination condition, which can lead to infinite loops and out-of-gas failures. Practical guidance: ensure any while loop has a clearly bounded number of iterations and prefer deterministic for loops when possible. When dealing with collections, prefer batch processing across multiple transactions or using off-chain computation with on-chain verification. The hands-on activity in this chapter asks you to implement an admin-only action with a guard; use that pattern to protect critical state changes from unexpected loops. Takeaway: while loops are powerful but must be proven to terminate in bounded steps to be safe in smart contracts.

keyIdea.title: Bounded while loops
keyIdea.text: Guarantee termination and bounds for while loops; otherwise prefer safer patterns like batched processing or mappings.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › While Loops
Countdown example
function countdown(uint _start) public pure returns (uint) {
  uint i = _start;
  uint total = 0;
  while (i > 0) {
    total += i;
    i--;
  }
  return total;
}
This is safe because i decreases each iteration and will reach zero deterministically.
Warning

If the loop condition depends on external state that might not change, the loop could run until gas is exhausted and revert.

Safer patterns
  • Batch processing across multiple transactions
  • Maintain aggregates incrementally instead of scanning
  • Use mappings for membership checks to avoid iteration
Key Takeaway

Never rely on unproven termination conditions. Prefer deterministic or bounded loops and consider off-chain work where appropriate.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Operators
screens.subtitle: Compact reminders of the most important operator ideas

narration.text: These concept cards summarize the operator rules you will return to frequently. Arithmetic operators perform numeric computations and in modern Solidity automatically revert on overflow and underflow, which protects state but requires careful testing. Comparison operators yield boolean results and form the basis of access checks and validation. Logical operators combine booleans and short-circuit, so order operands by cost and never expect side effects in skipped operands. Bitwise operators let you pack flags into a single integer for storage efficiency, but they reduce readability and demand clear documentation. Keep these short rules in mind as you design expressions: correctness first, then gas-aware ordering and compactness where it matters. screens.title: Key Concepts — Control Flow & Gas
screens.subtitle: Practical rules to avoid vulnerabilities and reverts

narration.text: Control flow and loops are where many on-chain failures happen. The essential rules are: prefer bounded loops or alternatives, use mappings for membership checks instead of scanning arrays, and design conditionals to fail early and remain audit-friendly. For loops and while loops consume gas per iteration and can cause transactions to revert if they become large or infinite. Practical alternatives include maintaining incremental aggregates when adding or removing items, providing functions that process fixed-size slices, and letting users claim or process items one-by-one. The hands-on challenge in this chapter—implementing an admin guard and an isAdmin check—reinforces how comparisons and conditionals secure actions. Remember: design for both correctness and gas predictability. In practical terms, practical rules to avoid vulnerabilities and reverts. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.
